title: Macklemore vs. the Owners' Box
dek: A Capitol Hill rapper said two words in a football stadium, a billionaire picked up the phone, and the biggest tour on earth lost its opener. Then he booked his own. The full story of five weeks that turned a pop tour into a referendum on Gaza.
body: Ben Haggerty has never been good at keeping his mouth shut, and Seattle loves him for it. The kid from Capitol Hill rapped about gay marriage when it cost him, rapped about addiction while he was still in it, and in May 2024 dropped "Hind's Hall," named for the Columbia University building protesters renamed after Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old killed in Gaza City that January. Every dollar of profit went to UNRWA. So nobody here was surprised when he walked onto a stadium stage in New Jersey this September and did it again. What surprised people was the bill.
## Two nights in New Jersey

Macklemore was confirmed as an opener on Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour in late August. On Friday, September 4, at MetLife Stadium, he wore a keffiyeh and performed "Hind's Hall" in front of images of a destroyed city.
> The people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them. (Macklemore, Sept. 4)

According to The Wall Street Journal, NFL owners complained after that show and were assured he'd drop the Palestine references the next night. Nobody has said who gave that assurance. On Saturday he went further. He told the crowd he wanted to say two words on stages across America, then said them: Free Palestine. And he spoke directly to Jewish fans.
> criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. (Macklemore, Sept. 5)

The crowd split. Some cheered. Some Jewish and Israeli fans walked out during his set and came back for Sheeran. A fan told CBS New York the video made Israeli soldiers look like Nazis; that's her description. Israel's Channel 12 reported two teenage girls left in tears. Macklemore posted the clip on September 7 with a one-line caption: wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial.
## The petition and the phone call

The Israeli-American Council launched a petition on September 6 telling Sheeran it was a concert, not a political rally, and demanding accountability. The ADL called the comments completely unacceptable. StopAntisemitism said fans deserved refunds, and Pink reshared that post.

Then came the call that ended it. According to the Journal, Patriots owner Robert Kraft, 85, spent 40 minutes on the phone with Sheeran. Kraft told him that calling Gaza a genocide is hate speech, said he sympathized with Palestinians but saw Hamas as the real problem, and said the shows at his Gillette Stadium would be canceled if Macklemore stayed. Kraft also named three other NFL owners who shared his position: David Tepper, Arthur Blank and Jeffrey Lurie. None of them has said so publicly.
On September 14, promoter Messina Touring Group announced Macklemore was off the remaining U.S. dates. He had been booked for 8 of the last 10.
## "I didn't need 10 shows from Ed. I needed 2."

Macklemore's statement that day ran long and pulled no punches. He called Sheeran a friend of 13 years and a brother. He said Sheeran told him Kraft wouldn't allow him in the stadium, and that Kraft rallied other owners behind an ultimatum. He said their talks ended in fundamental disagreement.
> There is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed. (Macklemore, Sept. 14)
> Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. (Macklemore, Sept. 14)

Then he said he'd already lost all of those things, and that he wasn't the victim, Sheeran wasn't the victim, Pink wasn't the victim. The victims, he wrote, are the Palestinian people. The two MetLife nights, he said, were the whole point: two chances to stand in front of 90,000 people.
## Kraft's side

Kraft answered the same day. Gillette events, he said, should not be a platform for hate speech, and Macklemore's participation would cross that line. He pointed to material shared from the stage and to what he called a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery. He also said this:
> I agree with Macklemore. Too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering. (Robert Kraft, Sept. 14)

He offered to sit down with Macklemore. That meeting hasn't happened. Context matters here: Kraft founded the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism in 2019 with $20 million, now called the Blue Square Alliance Against Hate, which bought this year's $15 million Super Bowl ad. He has been one of Israel's most prominent American backers for decades.
## Ed in the middle

Sheeran posted on September 15: the call was the promoter's, not his, the venue and promoter decision was final, and he wasn't complicit. Four days later in Philadelphia, with no opening act and reading from a teleprompter, he went further than anyone expected.
> What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate. (Ed Sheeran, Sept. 19)

He said he was making mistakes and was sorry, that he never wanted to be an activist musician, and that it had been one of the worst weeks of his life. Outside, protesters urged fans to get refunds. A week later his Gillette shows were canceled anyway, by a nor'easter.
## Everybody quits

By September 15 every remaining opener had walked. Finneas said artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed. Lukas Graham said money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Irish singer Aaron Rowe said Irish people know all too well about genocide, forced famine and occupation. The Irish band Beoga, founding members of Irish Artists for Palestine, said they understand colonialism. Sheeran replaced them with The Fray's Isaac Slade.
## Pick a side, celebrity edition

Pink said she was standing up for her own people and that a repost isn't a statement; a petition to strip her UNICEF ambassador role passed 150,000 signatures, and she still holds it. Boy George first said Sheeran had no spine, then called the openers who quit spineless rats. Colin Kaepernick said NFL owners were openly colluding. Greta Thunberg said you cannot be neutral in a genocide. Billy Bragg called Sheeran a hapless wimp who abandoned his friends at a billionaire's bidding. Lewis Hamilton thanked Macklemore for using his voice. In Gaza, artists painted murals of him on bombed-out walls.
## The money

On September 16 Macklemore pledged $1 million, his entire net from the Loop Tour, to six groups: the Palestine Children's Relief Fund, HEAL Palestine, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, UNRWA USA and Anera. He dared Kraft to match it.

Kraft said Sheeran had pledged $2 million of his own and asked him to match that for humanitarian aid in the region. Outlets split on whether Kraft actually committed; KIRO 7 noted he never explicitly did, and no recipients have been named. The next day Ms. Rachel, the toddler YouTube queen, matched Macklemore's million for the Palestine Children's Relief Fund. Billboard data showed "Hind's Hall" jumped from about 5,000 U.S. streams a day to about 87,000.
## Seattle has seen this movie

This isn't the first time a Free Palestine moment cost him. On September 21, 2024, at the Palestine Will Live Forever festival at Seward Park, he led a profane chant against America. The Kraken and Sounders, where he's a minority investor, called it increasingly divisive, the Mariners skipped "Can't Hold Us" at their next home game, and Las Vegas's Neon City Festival dropped him. He apologized for slipping up in the moment. And back in 2014, he wore a wig and fake nose at a surprise EMP show that critics called a Jewish stereotype; he said that never crossed his mind. His critics bring up both every time. His defenders point out he said from the MetLife stage, twice, that his target is a government, not a people.

Here at home, The Stranger's Audrey Vann wrote that as long as Macklemore advocates to end what she called Israel's genocide, she'll advocate for him. The city's establishment has mostly kept quiet this time.
## Meanwhile, in Gaza

The thing everyone's fighting about hasn't stopped. A ceasefire took effect October 10, 2025, and every living hostage taken in the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, which killed about 1,200 people in Israel, is home; the last remains came back in January. But Gaza's health ministry counts more than 1,500 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire and more than 74,000 since the war began. The UN has verified a lower number for the ceasefire period, and Israel disputes the ministry's figures. Israel still holds roughly two-thirds of the Strip. More than 100 aid groups say the ceasefire exists in name only, about 1.4 million people face crisis-level hunger, and food aid is shrinking this month for lack of money.
## The encore

On September 24 Macklemore announced his own Free Palestine Tour, every dollar to 12 groups including Anera, PCRF, UNRWA USA, Medical Aid for Palestinians and Jewish Voice for Peace. Dublin's 3Arena on October 26, Paris on October 29, London's OVO Arena Wembley on October 30. All three sold out almost immediately. U.S. dates, he says, are coming.
> It's 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn't work anymore. (Macklemore)
## The Sinner's take

Love him or hate him, the man did the most Seattle thing possible. He said the quiet part on the loudest stage in America, lost the gig, gave away the check and booked his own room. Kraft did what billionaires do and made a phone call. Sheeran tried to stand in the middle of a war and found out there's no middle. You can argue all day about the slogan, and you will.
So, Sinners: hero, hypocrite, or a guy who finally found a cause bigger than a thrift shop? When this tour comes home, does Climate Pledge sell out in minutes too? Argue below.
